description: Patient needs in Italy against the responses documented, proposed and measured in the sources.

title.text: What people with lupus in Italy need, and what the sources show
subtitle: Bars: share of respondents who flagged each need. Each bar comes from a different survey question, so compare within a row, not across rows. Circles: whether a
response is documented, proposed, and whether the gap itself is measured. Select a row to read the evidence. Sources: Lupus Europe Swiss Knife Survey 2024
(Italy), PaLESiamoci survey (Italy, n=151), LUNET registry protocol.

legend.labelExpr: {'solid':'Documented as in place','light':'Planned, proposed or partly measured','empty':'Nothing found, so we cannot tell'}[datum.label]

values.detail: The LUNET registry protocol lists 18 referral centres with defined SLE expertise. It is a protocol, not a measure of access. Earlier Italian registries were LIRE (2015–2021) and the Early Lupus Project.
56% of respondents ask for more specialised centres. The PaLESiamoci authors also call for more awareness of lupus among general practitioners to speed up diagnosis.

Respondents report 2.7 years on average to diagnosis, 20% travelling far for specialist care and over a third of follow-up visits being private. How many patients live near an SLE centre is not measured.

No source documents a multidisciplinary service as in place. Patients and clinicians define the term differently: patients mean seeing several specialists, clinicians mean specialists discussing cases together.
Coordinated pathways with continuity of contact and a shared definition of multidisciplinary care (patients and the advisory board).
44% say they are managed by a multidisciplinary team. How many centres offer one is not measured.
Psychological support exists but only 20% of PaLESiamoci respondents had it early in the disease; 80% said they were not referred. LUNET plans to record anxiety and depression with the HADS scale.
Psychological support built into SLE care pathways (advisory board and analyst).
Early referral is measured (20%), but the share of people who need support, and later access, is not.
Belimumab, anifrolumab and voclosporin are described as approved. Reimbursement and access in Italy are not covered. LUNET plans to track adverse reactions.
Steroid-sparing treatment in line with EULAR 2023 advice, plus open discussion of risks (advisory board).
64% were on corticosteroids (96% in the severe group). Whether use is falling, or how easily newer drugs can be reached, is not measured.
The LUNET protocol records fatigue impact with the MFIS scale. A plan, no results yet.
Structured access to exercise, nutrition and lifestyle support (advisory board). 40.4% also name access to non-drug treatments as an unmet need.
No source shows what fatigue or lifestyle support exists in Italy, or whether it helps.
Belimumab is described as approved for lupus nephritis and voclosporin as approved. LUNET plans to profile lupus nephritis and monitor heart and bone health.
Education on how irreversible organ damage can be (advisory board). Patients focus on current symptoms; clinicians stress long-term risk.
Screening and monitoring coverage in Italy is not measured. Kidney is also the top worry today (30.6%) and long term (35.8%).
Law 104 benefits exist, but respondents ask for easier access. How many eligible people use them is not measured.
Financial support for therapy-related costs and easier access to Law 104 benefits (patients: 61% and 29%).
Out-of-pocket follow-up costs averaged more than €700 a year. What share of total cost is covered is not measured.
LUNET plans to record patient-reported measures (HAQ, EQ-5D-5L, MFIS, HADS) at enrolment and yearly. A plan, no results yet.
Stronger rheumatologist–patient communication and tailored educational materials (advisory board).
In the Swiss Knife Survey 18.2% of Italian respondents most miss attention to what cannot be measured (Europe 25.0%). Whether clinics record fatigue or mood routinely is not measured.
